title: Public investment can be a formalization gateway only if the project outlives itself
source_unit: International Labour Organization, Promoting formalization outcomes in Employment-Intensive Investment Programme, ILO Brief, August 2026
geography: Employment-Intensive Investment Programme contexts in low- and middle-income countries, with illustrative cases from the Philippines and Central African Republic

denominator.unit: global and low-income-country informality frame used by the guidance brief

global_scale.value: nearly 2 billion workers make their living in the informal economy

low_income.unit: percent of total employment informal in low-income countries, with rural informal employment at 93.7% in the cited 2019 frame

construction.unit: approximately percent of construction workers informal in low- and middle-income countries in the cited 2019 comparison

project_afterlife.value: EIIP projects commonly improve working and living conditions during infrastructure and rural-work interventions, but workers and economic units often remain informal or revert to informality when projects conclude

mechanism.value: temporary public investment can create a formalization gateway, but project duration, labor-market conditions, weak data and limited institutional capacity determine whether the gateway remains open after completion

observations.method: ILO guidance brief synthesizing global informality indicators, EIIP programme experience, formalization meta-analyses, and illustrative project evidence.
observations.uncertainty: The brief is a practice and policy synthesis rather than a harmonized impact evaluation; cited informality figures use different years and frames, and reversion to informality is described as a recurring challenge rather than estimated as a universal rate.
observations.subgroup: Informal workers and economic units in construction, rural works, low-income countries, public employment programmes, and communities receiving infrastructure investment.
observations.counterinterpretation: Temporary employment can still produce valuable income, skills, assets and social-protection contact even if formal status is not sustained; reversion may reflect the surrounding labor market rather than project failure alone.

observations.period: 2020–2026; formalization pathways and illustrative public-employment cases

denominator.unit: ILO EIIP formalization intervention and case-study frame

intervention_set.value: effective pathways combine information and training, simplified administration, social-security and tax incentives, compliance, enforcement and financial incentives rather than relying on one tool

employment_nexus.value: worker registration tends to produce more substantial formalization outcomes than enterprise registration alone; social security and labor protections should be integrated with enterprise compliance

philippines_case.value: a Philippines community emergency employment programme provided 15 days of employment to informal workers in conflict-affected communities; more than 1,800 workers and nearly 12,000 households benefited, with social security, health, accident and third-party liability insurance linked to the work

car_case.value: a Central African Republic project built skills for about 100 young people, 28% women, and supported three construction cooperatives to access equipment, regulatory compliance and procurement pathways; follow-up funding and municipal capacity constrained scale-up

mechanism.value: formalization is more plausible when public employment bundles immediate income with worker registration, skills, collective organization, procurement access and a route into the next contract

observations.method: ILO synthesis of formalization meta-analyses and illustrative EIIP project cases; the cases are used to identify pathways and implementation conditions, not as comparable treatment effects.
observations.uncertainty: Case figures describe programme reach and design, not durable formal status, income, welfare or causal impact; the Philippines and Central African Republic examples differ in context, duration and outcome measurement.
observations.subgroup: Informal workers, conflict-affected communities, young men and women, community contractors, small construction cooperatives, local governments and public procurement actors.
observations.counterinterpretation: Insurance or registration attached to a short programme may protect workers during participation without creating lasting employment; cooperatives can improve access while remaining dependent on external procurement and follow-up finance.

observations.period: 2026 project-design guidance; measurement, procurement and institutional follow-through

denominator.unit: EIIP project design and monitoring framework

sustainability_constraints.value: weak governance, limited formal job demand, short project duration, overcrowded objectives, fiscal constraints, weak local capacity and insufficient informality data can prevent durable formalization

formalization_indicators.value: recommended indicators include enterprise and worker registration, contracts and social-security contributions, workdays of formal employment, wages, leave, revenue, assets, finance access and procurement contracts

procurement_route.value: projects can support informal entities through cooperative organization, tender information, bid preparation, business services and certification, while requiring formalization by project end where feasible

governance.value: formalization should be a core project objective, targeted by diagnosis and social dialogue, with indicators in monitoring and evaluation systems to trigger adaptive management

mechanism.value: infrastructure becomes a social contract only when the project records and funds the transition from temporary participation to durable rights, enterprise capability and market access

observations.method: Practice guidance based on formalization literature, EIIP theory of change, project cases and recommendations for project design, procurement and monitoring.
observations.uncertainty: The recommendations are not a tested package; achievable outcomes depend on national legislation, fiscal space, procurement rules, labor demand, local capacity and implementation duration.
observations.subgroup: Project designers, local governments, contractors, worker organizations, informal enterprises, public buyers, social-protection agencies and communities receiving public infrastructure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Adding formalization indicators can overload already complex infrastructure projects, and procurement requirements can exclude small informal units if support, finance and realistic sequencing are absent.

boundary: This record adds a project-afterlife and public-investment gateway layer to the formalization atlas. The brief is practice guidance and evidence synthesis, not a causal evaluation of EIIP, a universal reversion rate, or proof that social-protection linkage, cooperative organization, procurement access or indicators produce durable formal employment, wages, business growth, poverty reduction or worker wellbeing.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official ILO 12-page PDF and publication/topic pages, informality context, EIIP project-afterlife problem, intervention typology, worker-registration nexus, Philippines and Central African Republic examples, constraints, procurement pathway, indicators and recommendations were reviewed.
